title: Chapter 4 Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of services, dependency injection, and service patterns.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a service in Angular?
options: To encapsulate reusable logic and data sharing
questions.explanation: Services hold shared business logic, state, and operations that components can use.

questions.question: Which decorator is used to make a class injectable?
questions.explanation: `@Injectable()` marks a class as available to be injected with dependencies.

questions.question: You must always list a service in the `providers` array of `AppModule` to use it.
questions.explanation: If you use `providedIn: 'root'`, the service is automatically registered with the root injector.

questions.question: What does `providedIn: 'root'` accomplish?
options: Makes the service available only to the AppComponent
Registers the service at the root level so a single instance is shared app‑wide
Creates a new instance for every component
Imports the service from another module
questions.explanation: It provides the service as a singleton in the root injector, available everywhere.

questions.question: The Angular CLI command to generate a service is `ng generate ______ service-name`.
questions.explanation: The full command is `ng generate service name` or `ng g s name`.

questions.question: How do you inject a service into a component?
options: By adding it to the template
By declaring a constructor parameter with the service type
questions.explanation: Angular DI uses the constructor parameter type to determine what to inject.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `private` keyword in `constructor(private service: MyService) {}`?
options: It makes the service inaccessible outside the constructor.
It automatically creates and assigns a class property `service`.
It prevents the service from being injected.
It is required by Angular for injection to work.
questions.explanation: TypeScript parameter properties automatically create a class member with the same name.

questions.question: Two components that inject the same `providedIn: 'root'` service will receive two different instances.
questions.explanation: They share the same singleton instance.

questions.question: Where would you add a provider so that a component and its children get a dedicated instance of a service?
options: In the `providers` array of the component’s @Component decorator
questions.explanation: Component‑level providers create a new instance scoped to that component and its descendants.

questions.question: How does Angular resolve a dependency?
options: It searches the entire injector tree bottom‑up until found.
It only looks in the root injector.
It looks in the component’s injector first, then moves up to parent injectors.
It requires you to specify the provider location each time.
questions.explanation: Resolution goes from the current injector up the hierarchy to the root.

questions.question: Which provider type would you use to supply a pre‑configured constant object?
questions.explanation: `useValue` provides a static value directly.

questions.question: What is the advantage of using `async` pipe with an observable from a service?
options: It automatically subscribes and unsubscribes, preventing memory leaks.
It converts the observable into a promise.
It stores the observable in local storage.
questions.explanation: The async pipe manages the subscription lifecycle, avoiding manual cleanup.

questions.question: It’s a best practice to expose a Subject directly from a service so components can emit new values.
questions.explanation: Expose only the `.asObservable()` to prevent outside code from calling `.next()`.

questions.question: What does the `@Optional()` decorator do?
options: It tells Angular to inject `null` if the dependency is not found, instead of throwing an error.
It marks a service as not injectable.
questions.explanation: `@Optional()` prevents a `NullInjectorError` and injects `null` if no provider exists.

questions.question: Which RxJS class is ideal for holding the latest value in a service and replaying it to new subscribers?
questions.explanation: BehaviorSubject requires an initial value and emits the current value to new subscribers immediately.

questions.question: Why should you manually unsubscribe from an observable in `ngOnDestroy`?
options: Because the observable will stop emitting otherwise.
To prevent memory leaks caused by subscriptions that outlive the component.
It's required by Angular for change detection.
There is no need to unsubscribe; Angular handles it automatically.
questions.explanation: Active subscriptions that aren’t cleaned up can cause memory leaks and unexpected behavior.

questions.question: What does the Angular CLI create when you run `ng generate service my-service`?
options: A service class file and a test file
A module that contains the service
questions.explanation: It generates `my-service.service.ts` and `my-service.service.spec.ts`.

questions.question: The DI mechanism that creates a service instance and passes it to a component is called ________.
questions.explanation: Angular uses constructor injection to supply dependencies.

questions.question: A service with `providedIn: 'root'` will be included in the final bundle only if:
options: It is actually injected somewhere in the app.
It has at least one method.
questions.explanation: Tree‑shaking removes unused services. If no component injects it, it’s excluded from the bundle.

questions.question: Services can only contain methods; they should never store state.
questions.explanation: Services can (and often do) hold application state that multiple components share.
